metadata.title: Claude, Hiring Review.
metadata.subtitle: What a Skill Actually Is
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: does Claude gain hiring judgment when it picks up the hiring-review skill? Take the skill apart, explain the read-then-execute mechanism, name the trade-off (same checklist every time, and no opinion off the map), and land the carry-out that a skill is a file of steps Claude reads before it starts — not new decision-making power.

beats.narration_text: People hear 'hiring-review skill' and read it as: Claude gained hiring judgment. Wrong branch. Nothing in the model moved — it was handed a file to walk through. So what's actually inside that file?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('decides' -> 'checks') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: Say 'Claude has a hiring-review skill' and it sounds like an upgrade to the model itself — as if training added a new capability, and Claude now knows, in its own head, how to screen candidates and decide who moves forward. That's the natural read. It's also the wrong one.

Here's the tell. Delete the skill's folder from disk and rerun the same prompt — Claude doesn't lose any hiring judgment, because there wasn't any to lose. It just stops following that one written checklist. The judgment lived in the file, not in the model.

Here's what a skill actually is, stripped of the branding: one folder, and inside it, one file. Hiring-review is a directory that holds a single SKILL.md — plain-English instructions for walking a hiring decision step by step, which Claude reads top to bottom before it does anything else.

The execution model is deliberately dumb. Claude reads the file top to bottom and works through the steps in the order they're written — no branching, no re-ordering, unless the file itself explicitly says branch. Linear by design.

That's why a skill is a specification, not new judgment. They optimized for repeatability — the same checklist runs on every review, every time, no drift. What it costs you: anything outside those written steps, Claude has no special opinion about. Off the map means back on you.

So hiring-review never handed Claude the judgment for who to hire. What it guarantees is narrower, and more useful: every time you invoke it, Claude reads the same file and follows the same checklist. That's the whole mechanism. That's also the whole trick.

beats.narration_text: The failure mode cuts both ways. Watching Claude flag every risk in a hire doesn't prove it understood the situation — a checklist can run to the letter and still miss whatever the author didn't include. And watching it flag nothing doesn't prove the hire is clean — it may just be a case the file doesn't cover. What you see is that the checklist ran, not that the checklist was complete.

A skill named hiring-review doesn't hand Claude the judgment for who to hire — it's a file of steps Claude reads before it starts, so the same checks run every review, and anything outside those steps is still on you.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: pick one decision I check the same way every time — before an offer goes out, before a candidate moves to the next round. Write me a SKILL.md for it — plain language, ordered steps — then read it back to me and walk me through exactly what you'll check, before you check it. Go deeper: hand the same model a candidate whose situation doesn't fit any step on your list and ask where it silently starts filling in judgment you never wrote down — because that's the seam where a hiring-review quietly stops being a checklist and starts pretending to be a decision.
